statedGuarantee: Sandlock confines a whole process tree launched from an unprivileged developer account (no root, no cgroups, no images, no mandatory namespaces). Policy is split: input-independent invariants (readable/writable path prefixes, denied paths, TCP port scope, IPC scope, unconditional syscall denials) are compiled into Landlock (ABI 6+) and seccomp-bpf and enforced by the kernel; runtime-dependent decisions (resolved connect destination, HTTP method/host/path, execve argv, filesystem effects to be captured rather than applied, process and memory accounting) are routed through a seccomp user-notification supervisor in the trusted parent, which replies Allow / Deny(errno) / Continue and can act on behalf of the child via pidfd_getfd. Additional claims: endpoint hostnames resolved once and pinned (no DNS rebinding); a TOCTOU-safe programmable runtime hook (policy_fn) that can tighten kernel-enforced policy live; unprivileged copy-on-write workspaces with commit/abort/dry-run; and a pipeline operator giving each stage its own confinement so that dual-LLM / CaMeL-style capability separation is enforced by the kernel rather than by the model. Fail-closed by construction: where neither layer can decide soundly, the operation is denied.
advertisedRhetoric: "static, input-independent policy is compiled into kernel-enforced rules, while a narrow supervisor handles runtime-dependent decisions and virtualized effects"; "Landlock (Salaün, 2017) provides the kernel-enforced “static” layer of policy"; "the capability separation a prompt-injection-resistant decomposition relies on is enforced by the kernel rather than trusted to the LLM’s judgment"; "an unprivileged, kernel-enforced substrate on which the separated stages run". The authors notably do NOT overclaim: they scope out kernel vulnerabilities and side channels, call argv inspection "not a containment boundary", and concede cgroups remain stronger for adversarial resource exhaustion.
tierSpan: Sandlock uses it for constraints whose verdict is independent of syscall-time data: filesystem read/write scope, TCP port scope, and IPC boundaries. When a rule can be expressed this way, common operations are denied or allowed by the kernel without involving the supervisor.
cheapestDefeat: TIER WORK, EXPLICIT. (1) Guarantee: a confined process tree cannot read or write outside granted path prefixes, cannot reach a network endpoint outside the pinned allowlist, cannot exceed process/memory caps, and cannot escape confinement by forking or exec-ing. (2) Mechanism that must fail: the Landlock LSM domain plus the seccomp-bpf filter, both installed after PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS and both inherited across fork() and execve(), together with the seccomp user-notification supervisor running in the trusted parent. (3) Cheapest adversary action: there is no in-sandbox software bypass on offer — after NO_NEW_PRIVS the filter cannot be shed, descendants inherit it, and the design fails closed ('If freezing or creation tracking is unavailable (e.g. Yama blocks ptrace), the syscall is denied with EPERM rather than silently relaxed'). The cheapest defeats are therefore (a) an over-broad grant by the policy author — the writable prefix that happens to contain the agent's own config or an SSH-agent socket, or an allowlisted host that will proxy arbitrary traffic — and (b) a kernel/LSM vulnerability, which the paper explicitly places out of scope: 'Kernel-level vulnerabilities, side channels, and resource-exhaustion attacks against shared kernel structures are out of scope.' (4) Tier of the mechanism those actions defeat: the kernel-level reference monitor (Landlock LSM hooks + seccomp) = T2. Misconfiguration and kernel vuln are precisely the canonical T2 defeats, not T3 chokepoint evasion: even the supervisor-mediated classes are reached because the kernel traps the syscall, so there is no 'path that does not traverse the chokepoint' for the classes routed to notification. This is a genuine T2 anchor, not a T3 advertised as T2.
placementSpan: We assume the sandboxed process may execute attacker-influenced code or consume attacker-controlled data, including package scripts, downloaded files, tool outputs, and generated commands. The host kernel, the Sandlock supervisor, and the embedding agent runtime are trusted; kernel vulnerabilities, side channels, privileged local attackers, and deliberate exhaustion of global kernel resources are out of scope.

coverageSpans.E1: Filesystem policy grants read and write capabilities over host paths and can attach an effect action to writes: COMMIT merges captured changes, ABORT discards them, and KEEP leaves them for inspection.
coverageSpans.E2: Fork-like syscalls (clone, fork, vfork, and clone3) are traced for one ptrace creation event so children are registered before user code runs; for clone3, Sandlock reads flags from the clone-argument structure. If freezing or creation tracking is unavailable (e.g. Yama blocks ptrace), the syscall is denied with EPERM rather than silently relaxed.
coverageSpans.E3: Concrete hostnames are resolved once at sandbox start and pinned for the child process, eliminating DNS-rebinding attacks. Wildcard hostnames are intentionally outside the model: every allowed domain must resolve to a concrete destination that the supervisor can check.
coverageSpans.E4: ‡Method/host/path control over HTTPS requires installing a sandbox CA in the workload; without it, HTTPS is governed by pinned-endpoint allowlisting.
coverageSpans.E5: An npm install step legitimately needs network access and writes under node_modules that the test step it sets up should not retain; the transition between the two is observable (the execve of the test runner) but not expressible as a single static ruleset over one invocation.
coverageSpans.E6: Sandboxes run alongside the developer’s editor, SSH keys, and source trees. Confinement must be unprivileged (developer accounts rarely have free use of sudo) and must default-deny the rest of the home directory.
coverageSpans.E7: Process count. Fork-like syscalls are gated by a counter; thread creation (CLONE_THREAD) is excluded, and excess processes receive EAGAIN.

schneider.surrogate: A per-process-tree syscall-and-resource safety property enforced by an actual execution monitor: no open/read/write outside the granted path prefixes, no connect/send to an endpoint outside the pinned allowlist, no fork past the process cap, no mmap/brk past the address-space cap, no syscall outside the permitted set. Landlock and seccomp ARE reference monitors in the Schneider sense, and the Table 3 effectiveness micro-evaluation confirms all ten deny/allow cases behaved as the policy requires.
schneider.objective: Prompt-injection resistance via capability separation — that private data never reaches an externally-communicating component (the 'lethal trifecta'). That is an information-flow hyperproperty over multiple executions and is not enforceable by an execution monitor. The paper is unusually explicit that its surrogate does not deliver it: 'Sandlock bounds stage capabilities, not pipe content: a compromised upstream stage can still shape bytes consumed downstream, so data-provenance defenses (Debenedetti et al., 2025) remain complementary. Second, sound decompositions remain the author’s responsibility: Sandlock kernel-enforces the separation specified, but does not prove that the untrusted-content stage never needs network or that the networked stage never needs private data.'

Authors: Cong Wang (Multikernel Technologies, Inc.) and Yusheng Zheng (UC Santa Cruz). ~7K lines of Rust, open source at github.com/multikernel/sandlock. Every span in this file is copied verbatim from that render; LaTeXML math artifacts (the doubled '~\sim' and 'x\times' sequences) were avoided when choosing spans, and curly apostrophes/quotes are preserved as rendered.

WHY THIS IS A CLEAN T2 ANCHOR. Unlike the many agent-security systems that advertise kernel strength while enforcing at an in-process hook or an application proxy, Sandlock's boundary really is the kernel and really is inherited. The confinement pipeline sets PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS, then Landlock, then the seccomp filter, all before exec; a descendant cannot shed them, so the DEPTH RULE is satisfied for E1/E2/E3/E5 by construction rather than by assertion. Even the runtime-decision classes are not a bypassable chokepoint: the syscall is trapped by the kernel filter, so there is no code path to the effector that avoids the supervisor. Equally useful for the corpus, the rhetoric is calibrated — the authors name argv matching as 'an observation and policy-tightening signal, not a containment boundary', concede cgroups are stronger for adversarial exhaustion, and scope out kernel vulns. Under the weakest-link rule this scores exactly where it advertises, which is rare.

WHERE I WAS UNCERTAIN, AND WHY I STILL SCORED CHARITABLY.
1) io_uring. The paper never mentions io_uring, the classic seccomp-evasion path for file and network work. Landlock is LSM-hook-based so filesystem and TCP scope would still bind, but the SUPERVISOR-mediated classes (COW capture, HTTP rules, UDP/ICMP on-behalf) could in principle be reached through a ring without a seccomp trap. I did not downgrade on this, because the text says the filter 'denies syscalls outside Landlock’s scope' and the charitable reading is that io_uring_setup sits in the deny set. An adjudicator wanting the adversarial reading should treat this as the single strongest candidate for knocking E3 and E5 down to partial.
2) E3 covered rather than partial. Every egress syscall from the agent or any descendant is either Landlock-enforced (TCP ports, direct path), supervisor-validated against the pinned allowlist (host rules, UDP, ICMP, HTTP), or denied. The HTTPS caveat is a GRANULARITY limit — method and path are invisible without the sandbox CA — not a mediation gap, since the endpoint itself is still checked; so it does not trigger the covert-channel rule for E3 as that effector is defined. The genuine information-flow leak (an untrusted stage shaping bytes that a networked SIBLING stage then sends) is not egress 'by the agent or any descendant' of that stage, so I routed it to the Schneider split rather than to E3. A reviewer who reads E3 as covering data-controlled-by-the-agent leaving the machine would legitimately mark E3 partial on that caveat.
3) E4 partial. VCS push is never named in the paper. It decomposes into spawn plus egress, both mediated, so a push to a host outside the allowlist is genuinely refused — real coverage. But it provably fails to reach the instances that matter: any working dev allowlist contains the forge host, and once it does, a push of any content to any repo on that host proceeds. Path-level rules cannot rescue this by default because git-over-HTTPS needs the sandbox CA installed in the workload and git-over-SSH is opaque TCP the supervisor cannot parse at all. Reaches some, provably not others = partial.
4) E6 partial by the DEPTH RULE, and I would cap it there regardless. Filesystem-borne credentials are well covered (default-deny of the home directory; the threat model names SSH keys explicitly; the policy_fn example denies /etc/shadow), and the cloud metadata endpoint is covered by default-deny egress. But NO credential list is published anywhere in the paper, which alone caps at partial — and separately there is no mention of environment sanitization anywhere in the text: a token already in the parent's environ is inherited across fork/exec into the sandbox and is then usable against any allowlisted endpoint.
5) E7 partial. Sandlock has no concept of an agent, only of processes. A sub-agent spawned as an OS process is fully mediated (same clone/fork/clone3 interception, same inherited confinement, same process cap). A sub-agent that is a THREAD is not — CLONE_THREAD is explicitly excluded from the counter — and a sub-agent invoked by calling a model API over an allowlisted endpoint is invisible to the sandbox entirely. Some instances, provably not others = partial. Not not-covered, because the OS-process case is real and enforced.
6) Placement. Primary A2 because the threat model's attacker arrives as attacker-controlled data and content (package scripts, downloaded files, tool outputs, generated commands) that then executes inside the confined child, and because that is what the Table 3 effectiveness checks actually exercise — including 'Untrusted stage reads private data -> denied', which directly tests the prompt-injection decomposition. Secondary A3 (generated-not-known-in-advance agent behavior, addressed via policy_fn phase transitions and per-stage confinement but never tested against an actually misaligned model) and A5 (supply chain: the npm/package-hook case is addressed by design; note the OTHER half of A5 — kernel and hypervisor — is explicitly OUT of scope, not merely untested). A4 does not apply in the paper's own terms, since the supervisor and the embedding agent runtime are declared trusted.
7) Evidence grade L2, not L3. Table 3 is a genuine behavioral confirmation of ten deterministic deny/allow cases and the benchmarks are measured, so this sits above L1 source inspection. But the effectiveness evaluation is a compliance test, not an adversarial one — no red team, no attempted escape — and the authors flag that 'A systematic compatibility study across the long tail of agent tooling is future work'. No reproducible bypass is demonstrated, so not L3.
8) One honest caveat that does NOT affect any effector cell: memory accounting bounds address space requested via mmap/mremap/brk/shmget rather than resident pages, and the authors say so plainly ('for adversarial workloads aiming to exhaust kernel memory through corner-case syscalls, cgroups remain stronger'). Resource exhaustion is not an ACTION-SURFACE-v1.1 effector, so it is recorded here rather than scored.
9) Deployment precondition worth flagging for any T2 comparison table: the whole guarantee requires Landlock ABI 6, i.e. Linux 6.12 or newer, and Sandlock refuses to run below that floor rather than degrading. That is the right failure mode, but it means the T2 claim is unavailable on older kernels rather than weakened on them.
